blocks.text: Design a general e-commerce marketplace like Amazon, letting customers browse an enormous catalog, add items to a cart, and check out, while a single product can be fulfilled from any of several independent warehouses. The hard problem this design centers on is neither browsing nor payment, both largely solved elsewhere in this project, it is inventory itself: reserving stock across multiple warehouses without ever overselling a product, while still giving a genuine, in-progress checkout a fair window to complete, without letting an abandoned cart permanently lock away stock other customers could have bought.
blocks.content: Design a general e-commerce marketplace like Amazon, letting customers browse an enormous catalog, add items to a cart, and check out, while a single product can be fulfilled from any of several independent warehouses. The hard problem this design centers on is neither browsing nor payment, both largely solved elsewhere in this project, it is inventory itself: reserving stock across multiple warehouses without ever overselling a product, while still giving a genuine, in-progress checkout a fair window to complete, without letting an abandoned cart permanently lock away stock other customers could have bought.

blocks.alt: Adding an item to a cart reserves it from whichever warehouse has sufficient stock, with a time-limited hold that either converts to a real sale on checkout or releases the stock back automatically if it expires unclaimed

blocks.text: The two techniques that solve this are multi-warehouse inventory selection, checking candidate warehouses for a product in priority order and reserving from the first one with sufficient stock, and time-limited cart holds, reserving stock the moment it enters a cart but only for a bounded window, converting to a permanent sale on successful checkout or automatically releasing back to inventory if that window passes unclaimed.
blocks.content: The two techniques that solve this are multi-warehouse inventory selection, checking candidate warehouses for a product in priority order and reserving from the first one with sufficient stock, and time-limited cart holds, reserving stock the moment it enters a cart but only for a bounded window, converting to a permanent sale on successful checkout or automatically releasing back to inventory if that window passes unclaimed.

blocks.text: A customer should be able to browse a catalog and add items to a cart. Adding an item to a cart should reserve its inventory from an appropriate warehouse, without allowing the product to be oversold across all warehouses combined. A cart reservation that is never converted into a completed checkout within a reasonable window should automatically release its held inventory back. A completed checkout should convert its held reservation into a real, permanent order that is never released.

blocks.alt: Never oversell a product, fair access with no cart hoarding, correctness across many warehouses and sellers, fast browsing at enormous catalog scale, and trustworthy sellers and listings

blocks.text: Never overselling means two different customers must never both successfully complete a purchase for the very last unit of something. Fair access, no cart hoarding means simply adding an item to a cart and never actually checking out must not permanently block other customers from buying stock that is, in reality, still available. Correctness across many warehouses and sellers means the same product can genuinely be fulfilled from any of several independent inventory pools, not just one. Fast browsing at enormous catalog scale means viewing product listings has to stay fast regardless of how large the total catalog and inventory actually are. And trustworthy sellers and listings means a marketplace hosting many independent sellers needs real, active protection against fraudulent or counterfeit listings reaching real customers.

blocks.text: This design assumes payment processing reuses the payment system this project already covers, and focuses instead on what is genuinely central here, multi-warehouse inventory reservation. An extreme, single-instant demand surge, such as a flash sale for one specific, scarce item, is assumed out of scope, treated as a separate, dedicated design elsewhere in this category built around that far more extreme contention pattern. A cart hold is assumed to last a fixed, modest window, long enough for a genuine checkout attempt, short enough that an abandoned cart does not meaningfully lock away real stock.

blocks.text: A platform at real scale might list hundreds of millions of distinct products, with a single popular product often stocked across many independent warehouses. Cart additions vastly outnumber completed checkouts, since browsing and cart abandonment are both far more common than an actual purchase. A typical cart hold lasts on the order of minutes before expiring unclaimed if checkout never completes, long enough for a real customer to finish paying, short enough to avoid meaningfully starving other buyers of genuinely available stock.

blocks.text: A customer browses the catalog service and adds an item to their cart through the cart service, which asks the multi-warehouse inventory selector to reserve the needed quantity, checking candidate warehouses in priority order until one has sufficient stock. That reservation becomes a time-limited hold; completing checkout, through the payment system, converts it into a permanent order via fulfillment, while letting the hold simply expire releases the reserved stock back automatically.

blocks.alt: A cart addition triggers the inventory selector to reserve stock from the best candidate warehouse as a time-limited hold, converting to a permanent order on checkout or releasing back automatically if it expires unclaimed

blocks.text: When a customer needs a quantity of a product reserved, the best candidate warehouse, such as the nearest one to them, is checked first; if it has sufficient stock, the reservation is made there, otherwise the next best candidate warehouse is tried instead, continuing until one succeeds or every warehouse has been exhausted.

blocks.alt: A reservation checks the best candidate warehouse first and falls through to the next best one if it lacks sufficient stock, continuing until one succeeds or all have been exhausted

blocks.text: Adding an item to a cart reserves its inventory immediately, but only as a time-limited hold, not an outright, permanent sale. If checkout completes before that hold expires, the reservation converts into a real order; if it never completes, the hold expires and its reserved stock is automatically released back, available for other customers again.

blocks.text: Inventory is modeled per warehouse, per product, rather than as one combined, platform-wide stock count, since a reservation genuinely has to commit to one specific fulfilling warehouse, not an abstract, aggregated number. Cart holds are modeled as their own, separate, short-lived records rather than directly mutating a permanent order table, since a hold is explicitly a tentative, reversible state, unlike a completed order.

blocks.text: The happy path is the add-to-cart flow above, a clean reservation from the best available warehouse, held until checkout. The workflow worth walking through separately is a customer who adds an item to their cart and never returns, their hold sits reserved for its full duration, genuinely unavailable to anyone else during that window, but the moment it expires, the exact quantity they had held becomes available to other customers again, exactly the fairness guarantee that keeps an abandoned cart from permanently locking away real stock.

blocks.text: Catalog browsing is an ideal, heavy caching target, since the same popular product's listing page is viewed by an enormous number of different customers far more often than its underlying details actually change, unlike the inventory reservation decision itself, which always needs to read live, current stock.

blocks.text: Warehouse inventory is partitioned by product and warehouse, and replicated for durability, since a lost or duplicated reservation is a genuine, disruptive failure for a real customer. The catalog store is partitioned by product and heavily read-optimized, since it is read far more often than any single product's details actually change.

blocks.text: Relying on a background sweep as a safety net, rather than only an active, per-hold timer that could itself fail, is what guarantees an expired hold's stock is eventually released even if the primary expiry mechanism has some kind of transient failure.

blocks.text: Seller and listing trust is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since a marketplace hosting many independent, sometimes-unknown sellers has a real, ongoing risk of counterfeit goods or fraudulent listings that a single-seller retail model would never need to guard against.

blocks.text: Reservation retry and failure rate, per product, is the clearest signal of genuine, real-world inventory contention worth watching, a product retrying constantly during a specific window is a meaningful, actionable signal. Hold expiry rate is worth tracking too, an unusually high rate of unclaimed, expired holds for a specific product might point to a checkout friction problem worth investigating separately from inventory itself.

blocks.text: Time-limited cart holds are the right default because they are the only approach that gives a genuine, in-progress checkout real inventory protection while still guaranteeing an abandoned cart cannot lock stock away from other customers forever.

blocks.text: Heavy catalog caching is the largest read-side cost optimization here, since browsing volume vastly outweighs actual inventory-changing activity. Partitioning reservation logic by product, rather than a single, platform-wide inventory lock, avoids unnecessary coordination overhead for the overwhelming majority of products that never see genuine contention at all.

blocks.text: A change to cart hold duration needs careful, gradual rollout with real monitoring of both hold expiry rate and checkout completion rate, since too short a window frustrates genuine, slower checkouts, while too long a window worsens fairness for popular, contended products. Multi-warehouse selection logic changes deserve equal caution, a bug there risks either failing to find genuinely available stock or, worse, double-reserving the same units across two different warehouses.

blocks.text: Demand-aware, dynamic hold durations, shortening the window for an especially popular, low-stock product while keeping a longer, more forgiving window for ordinary items, would balance fairness and checkout friction more precisely than one fixed platform-wide duration. Smarter warehouse selection, weighing shipping cost and delivery speed alongside raw proximity, would improve fulfillment efficiency beyond today's simpler nearest-warehouse-first approach.

items: Architecture: multi-warehouse inventory reservation with time-limited cart holds, converting to a permanent order on checkout or releasing back automatically if unclaimed.
Capacity: hundreds of millions of products, a single popular product stocked across many warehouses, and cart additions vastly outnumbering completed checkouts.
The core techniques: multi-warehouse candidate fallback and time-limited cart holds, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a product-and-warehouse-partitioned inventory store alongside a short-lived cart hold store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal add-to-cart flow and an unclaimed hold expiry flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent, atomic reservation per warehouse, paired with an eventually consistent, cached catalog browsing experience.
Trade-offs: time-limited cart holds versus reserving only at checkout versus permanent, never-expiring reservations, compared directly on overselling protection and fairness against cart hoarding.
